paper_title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Frontier vision-language models are beginning to show remarkable capabilities in physical control. Recent studies of GPT-6 Astra demonstrate that general-purpose model can generate robot actions, perform manipulation, and improve its behavior through physical feedback [20, 80, 43]. What makes these results particularly intriguing is that such capabilities are not acquired primarily from robot demonstrations. Instead, they appear to draw on the broad knowledge developed during large-scale pretraining, including visual perception, spatial understanding, reasoning, and code generation [44, 11]. These observations suggest compelling possibility: the knowledge needed for more capable robot policies may already exist within frontier VLMs. Yet most vision-language-action models still rely on relatively small VLM backbones, such as the 2B Cosmos-Reason2 in GR00T N1.7 [58]. While effective, these models may not fully capture the rich knowledge emerging in frontier VLMs. This raises fundamental question: can frontier-scale representations unlock greater potential in learned robot policies? To investigate this question, we introduce ScaleVLA, which scales the VLM backbone of learned robot policy to 552 billion parameters using DeepSeek-V4.1Flash-1017 [15]. Inspired by the action-expert architecture of GR00T [4], we connect VLM to trainable diffusion transformer (DiT) that converts multimodal representations into continuous robot actions. Rather than relying on explicit reasoning at every control step, the policy learns to directly translate pretrained representations into actions. We systematically compare VLM backbones ranging from 2B to 552B parameters, holding the action architecture, initialization, robot demonstrations, and optimization budget fixed. This allows us to examine how much robot learning can benefit from stronger pretrained representations without introducing additional actionside supervision or pretrained robot-action experts. 1 Figure 1 ScaleVLA overview. Top left: backbone sizes. Top right: the VLM encodes images and the instruction, and the action DiT uses these features and robot state to generate an action chunk. Middle: task success by backbone size. Base is the best dense backbone at or below each size. Bottom: inference latency on RoboCasa, sample efficiency on LIBERO Goal, and success on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO. We argue that the value of robot foundation model should be measured not only by its performance on familiar tasks, but by how efficiently it learns, how well it generalizes, and how precisely it acts. We therefore evaluate ScaleVLA across LIBERO [47], LIBERO-PRO, RoboCasa [54], DexJoCo [74], and real-world manipulation, focusing on three fundamental capabilities. First, sample efficiency: on LIBEROGoal, ScaleVLA achieves 87.8% success with only 10 demonstrations per task, surpassing 2B backbone trained with 50 demonstrations (85.6%). Second, generalization: under LIBERO-PRO perturbations, it achieves 45.1% average success, compared with at most 31.3% for the smaller backbones, indicating stronger transfer beyond the training distribution. Third, precise manipulation: on real bimanual charger-insertion task, it succeeds in 9 out of 10 reference-layout trials, compared with 4 out of 10 for the 2B backbone. The improvement is concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment and insertion rather than reaching or grasping. Together, these results suggest that frontier representations are particularly valuable when robot data is scarce, the environment changes, or fine-grained coordination is required. Crucially, frontier-scale capacity does not necessarily imply prohibitive inference latency. DeepSeek-V4.1Flash uses sparse mixture-of-experts architecture, activating only fraction of its 552B parameters per token [14, 15]. Moreover, ScaleVLA extracts features from the causal encoder of the VLM without autoregressive reasoning or text generation. It achieves median inference latency of 216 ms per action chunk using four H200 GPUs  (table 6)  . This demonstrates that frontier VLM representations can support practical, subsecond robot control, although at higher hardware cost than smaller backbones. On the real robot, lower latency does not translate into faster execution: although ScaleVLA has the highest per-chunk latency of the three policies, it completes successful trials in median of 114.4 s, 13% less time than π0.5 + Action Head (132.0 s), because it aligns and inserts the plug 28% faster  (table 8)  . 2 Our findings point toward promising direction for VLA development. Frontier pretrained representations can substantially improve data efficiency, robustness, and contact-sensitive manipulation. Rather than treating frontier VLMs only as high-level reasoning agents, we show that they can serve as the representational foundation of fast, learned robot policies. We hope this work encourages shift toward fully exploiting frontier-model pretraining as central ingredient in building more capable and generalizable VLAs. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce ScaleVLA, VLA framework that connects 552B frontier VLM to trainable action DiT, enabling continuous robot control without autoregressive reasoning. We systematically investigate backbone scaling from 2B to 552B across simulation and real-world manipulation, demonstrating substantial gains in sample efficiency, generalization, and contactsensitive control. We demonstrate practical subsecond inference with sparse frontier VLM, showing that large pretrained representational capacity can be brought into learned robot policies at manageable latency.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: VLM as Policy. Language models select skills or write task plans [30, 27, 71]. PaLM-E conditions planning on sensor observations [17]. Other systems generate controller code, spatial value maps, or keypoint constraints for motion planning [44, 26, 28, 29]. Studies of Astra assess direct action generation, cooperation with learned policies, and improvement through feedback with fixed model weights [20, 80, 43]. Vision-Language-Action Models. Early policies learn from diverse tasks or multimodal prompts [65, 7, 32, 6, 34, 50]. Cross-embodiment policies extend this approach across robots [60, 22, 75, 16, 96, 8]. BridgeData V2 and DROID expand real robot data, MimicGen synthesizes demonstrations, and EgoDex provides egocentric hand trajectories [73, 35, 52, 25]. RT-2, OpenVLA, and FAST represent actions as tokens [101, 36, 62]. Continuous action chunks can be predicted by regression, diffusion, or flow matching [94, 37, 13, 39, 49, 5, 4]. Recent VLAs study open-world transfer [64, 21] and cross-embodiment alignment [84]. pretrained VLMs for imitation, GR00T N1.5 freezes them, and Knowledge Insulation separates actionexpert gradients from VLM adaptation [41, 56, 18]. Compact models and efficient action interfaces reduce training or inference cost [77, 48, 70, 76, 72]. Controlled comparisons revisit backbone choice, feature readout, and policy design [40, 89, 45, 81]. Demonstration sweeps test how much robot data adaptation requires [9]. We compare backbones up to 552B with fixed action DiT and demonstration budget. Spatial Reasoning for Robot Manipulation. Manipulation policies use language-conditioned spatial maps, multiview features, or point clouds [68, 69, 23, 24, 87]. Spatial supervision ranges from points and 3D references to action traces [11, 85, 98, 99, 83, 55]. Intermediate language, trace prompts, and highlevel trajectory predictions can guide action selection [86, 93, 2, 97, 42]. World Action Models. Video can specify task, supply visual subgoals, or provide synthetic demonstrations [31, 63, 33]. UniPi recovers actions from generated video [19]. Other approaches learn visual and action predictions together [78, 10, 95, 67, 59, 82, 38, 3]. DreamVLA forecasts perceptual features, DeFI separates forward and inverse dynamics, and ImageWAM uses image-editing features for control [90, 91, 92].

sections.title: 3.1 Model Architecture
sections.content: ScaleVLA has two parts (figure 2): frontier visionlanguage backbone that encodes the camera images and the language instruction, and an action head trained from scratch that turns these representations and the robot state into chunk of continuous actions with flow matching. Evaluations of GPT-6 Astra show useful manipulation through feedback-guided interaction and cooperation with learned policies, but repeated reasoning and action review make each decision slow and costly [20]. ScaleVLA does not reason in text: it reads the backbone once per action chunk and maps its representations directly to actions. The backbone supplies the knowledge of frontier-scale pretraining, and the action head learns continuous control from robot demonstrations. The language and visual backbones are frozen, while the feature adapter, state and action encoders, diffusion transformer, and action decoder are trainable. Visual pretraining supplies transferable features [53, 79, 51, 66], including DINOv2 and SigLIP features used in OpenVLA [61, 88, 36]. RoboFlamingo adapts Vision-language backbone. We adopt DeepSeek-V4.1Flash-1017 [15] as the vision-language backbone, mixture-of-experts model with 552B parameters. 3 Figure 2 ScaleVLA architecture. The VLM encodes the images and the instruction, and the action head reads the output of its causal encoder. The action DiT alternates cross-attention and self-attention and generates an action chunk in four flow steps. vision encoder converts camera images into visual tokens, and language backbone, organized into 20-layer causal encoder and 20-layer decoder, processes them together with the instruction in the reference chat format of the model. We run the causal encoder and read the features supplied to the attention operation of the next layer: sequence of visual and text tokens, each with Dvlm = 5120 dimensions. Computation stops at this interface, so the decoder never runs. We keep every token in order, with its modality label, so the action head can attend to image and non-image tokens separately. Action head. The action head follows the GR00T N1.7 architecture [58] and consists of feature adapter, state and action encoders, diffusion transformer (DiT), and an action decoder, all initialized randomly and trained on robot demonstrations. The feature adapter applies layer normalization and two-layer linear projection that maps each backbone token from Dvlm to common width of 2048, followed by four-layer self-attention transformer in which visual and language features interact under action supervision. Embodiment-specific multilayer perceptrons encode the robot state and the noisy actions, padded to common layout; each future action becomes token with learned position embedding, and the action encoder also receives the flow time. The action DiT has 32 layers that alternate self-attention and cross-attention. Self-attention runs jointly over the state and noisy action tokens, and cross-attention reads the adapted backbone features; successive cross-attention layers attend to non-image and image tokens in turn, and token masks exclude padding. Adaptive layer normalization supplies the flow time to the transformer, and an embodimentspecific action decoder maps the output action tokens to predicted velocity for the whole chunk. Across backbone comparisons, the action head keeps the same architecture and common random initialization; only the input width Dvlm of the feature adapter follows the backbone.

The loss averages squared error over valid action dimensions and timesteps. We normalize state and action values using the 1st and 99th percentiles of the training data. Gradients update only the action head, so we precompute the backbone features once and reuse them during training. Action chunk generation. At inference, the action head starts from Gaussian noise and integrates the predicted velocity in four steps to produce an action chunk. All four steps reuse the same backbone features, so the backbone runs once per chunk. We undo action normalization and execute the resulting numerical commands sequentially. ScaleVLA predicts 16step chunks for LIBERO, where eight commands are 4 executed before replanning, and 30-step chunks for DexJoCo. DexJoCo buffers timestamped commands and generates replacement chunks asynchronously while the controller executes available actions. This separates command execution from VLM inference. We measure execution rate and action-chunk latency separately to assess sustained control.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We compare policies with VLM backbones from 2B to 552B parameters. We measure task success in simulation, time policy inference, and vary the number of demonstrations to measure sample efficiency. We then evaluate the policies on bimanual robot.

sections.title: 4.5 Real-Robot Experiments
sections.content: Overview. To investigate whether the benefits of scaling VLM backbones extend beyond simulation, we conduct real-world experiments on bimanual robot. We use the Plug In Charger task from RoboDojo [12], which in our setup requires sequential execution of object grasping, bimanual handover, and precise, contact-rich insertion. This task provides challenging testbed for evaluating whether frontierscale visual representations can benefit both multistage manipulation and fine-grained robotic control. We further evaluate policy robustness under spatial perturbations and examine the practical feasibility of deploying frontier-scale VLA policy on physical robots. Training data. The task requires the right arm to grasp phone charger and hand it over, and the left arm to align the plug with power-strip socket, insert it, and release it, observed through top camera and two wrist cameras. We train on full teleoperated demonstrations and additional segments focused on insertion. Most demonstrations start near one reference charger position. Models. We compare three backbones under the same action DiT, training data, and training budget: Cosmos-Reason2-2B, π0.5 [64], and ScaleVLA. Each policy runs ten in-domain trials, which start near the dominant training position, and fifteen OOD trials, in which we shift or rotate the charger or move the power strip beyond most training placements. Success rates. As shown in table 8, ScaleVLA achieves the highest success rate under both indomain and OOD settings. Robot pretraining narrows but does not close the gap: π0.5 + Action Head succeeds in 8 of 10 in-domain and 7 of 15 OOD trials, compared with 9 of 10 and 8 of 15 for ScaleVLA, and needs median 81.2 rather than 58.1 to insert the plug. Notably, the benefits of frontier-scale representations are most evident in the contact-rich insertion stage. While all three policies exhibit comparable execution times during grasping and handover in successful trials, they differ substantially in their ability to align and insert the charger. All in-domain failures occur during insertion, whereas ScaleVLA completes this stage approximately 30% faster than the smallerbackbone policies. This suggests that scaling the VLM backbone can benefit not only high-level task understanding but also fine-grained manipulation that requires precise spatial perception and control. Under spatial distribution shifts, ScaleVLA maintains the highest success rate, although precise insertion outside the training distribution remains challenging. Interestingly, while the Cosmos-Reason2-2B policy encounters multiple safety stops due to insufficient arm clearance, ScaleVLA exhibits no such failures across all trials. Together, these observations suggest that frontier-scale pretrained representations can support more reliable visuomotor control in physically demanding manipulation tasks. Completion time and latency. Despite the increased inference latency of its frontier-scale backbone, ScaleVLA achieves the shortest end-to-end comple9 tion time among all evaluated policies  (table 8)  . This advantage primarily comes from more efficient execution of the contact-rich insertion stage. Interestingly, these results reveal that faster policy inference does not necessarily translate into faster task execution. For manipulation tasks requiring precise spatial alignment, improvements in action execution efficiency can outweigh the additional computational cost of scaling the backbone. This highlights the importance of evaluating the practical efficiency of VLA policies at the task level rather than solely through latency.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced ScaleVLA, which grounds the representations of 552B VLM in continuous robot actions through an action DiT trained with flow matching. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, RoboCasa, and DexJoCo, performance rises with backbone scale, and on real robot the 552B backbone inserts charger more reliably than the 2B backbone. Frontier features prove most valuable where robot data is scarce, conditions shift, or contact must be precise, and they remain fast enough for subsecond control, although on more hardware than smaller backbones. These results suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as the representational foundation of fast, learned robot policies.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: Feature extraction. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 supplies 5120-dimensional visual and text features at the causal encoderdecoder interface described in section 3.1. We retain the token sequence and modality labels, and cache the features for training. The smaller-backbone experiments use intermediate token representations with readout depth matched by common relative-depth rule. The previous comparison protocol uses layer round(16L/28) for an L-layer language model, giving readouts 16/28, 21/36, and 37/64 for the recorded 2B, 8B, and 32B backbones. Action head. The backbone features pass through layer normalization, two linear projections to width of 2048, and four layers of self-attention. The action DiT has 32 layers and alternates self-attention with cross-attention to the adapted features. State and noisy-action encoders, flow-time conditioning, and the embodiment-specific velocity decoder follow section 3.1. These action-side components are randomly initialized; no pretrained robot-action expert is loaded. The action DiT follows the GR00T N1.7 architecture [58]. Optimization and normalization. Policies are trained on 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (eight nodes with eight GPUs each), with global batch size of 640 and policy-training seed 42. For LIBERO, the initial fulldata recipe uses 5,000 AdamW steps at learning rate 104 with cosine decay and 5% warmup. The sampleefficiency experiment holds this training budget fixed and varies demonstrations per task  (table 7)  ; separate study varies update count at five demonstrations per task  (table 9)  . DexJoCo uses 20,000 optimizer steps at learning rate 104, with cosine decay and 5% warmup. State and action normalization uses the 1st and 99th percentiles of the corresponding training data. In the demonstration-budget sweep, policy updates use the selected subsets, but normalization retains statistics from the full training dataset. Thus, the reported demonstration counts describe trajectories used for policy updates, not all information used in preprocessing. Execution and Latency Measurement LIBERO predicts 16-step chunks and executes eight commands before obtaining the next policy decision. DexJoCo predicts 30-step chunks, assigns commands to execution timestamps, and computes replacement chunks while the controller consumes the buffer. Both run four flow steps using the backbone features from one forward pass per chunk. For each deployment setting, the timing report should specify hardware allocation, batch size, warmup, the number of timed calls, and whether other jobs run concurrently on the machine. Preprocessing, backbone inference, feature transfer, action-head inference, and postprocessing should be measured together for end-to-end chunk latency. Asynchronous execution. DexJoCo can continue executing buffered commands while the policy generates the next chunk. These commands may use older observations, so controller frequency alone does not measure how quickly the policy reacts to new feedback. To characterize the feedback loop, report chunk latency, observation age at execution, and intervals when the buffer has no valid commands. RoboCasa timing. Table 6 and figure 4 were measured on one machine with eight H200 GPUs, one request at time with batch size one. After 50 warm-up calls, each backbone handles 3,000 timed calls, made of 1,000 recorded RoboCasa observations (three camera images, robot state, and instruction) replayed three times. The observations come from rollouts of Cosmos-Reason2-2B policy on eight RoboCasa tasks. call is timed at the client, from sending the observation to receiving the action chunk. Client-side latency adds about 3 ms to the server time. The token counts in table 6 are typical input lengths per call. The measured median for ScaleVLA corresponds to 4.6 chunks per second for sequential requests. The server splits this time into backbone time, which includes message passing and preprocessing, and action-head time, which covers the feature adapter, four flow steps, and state and action processing. The action head predicts eight steps per chunk and runs without CUDA graphs on GPU that the backbone already uses. All backbones are served with vLLM 0.31 and the same settings: batch-invariant kernels, eager execution, and no prefix cache. Each model is cut at the readout layer used in training and runs one prefill pass per call. ScaleVLA uses four GPUs with tensor and expert parallelism, and the other backbones use one GPU. Each backbone uses its own RoboCasa Gen-100 checkpoint. vLLM serves for timing only: its features are not compared element by element with those of the Hugging Face deployment that produced the success rates. For every backbone except ScaleVLA, the prompt token ids and types of the two paths match on 16 observations. The single-GPU backbones were timed in four parallel lanes, one GPU each, while separate RoboCasa evaluation ran on 18 the other four GPUs. ScaleVLA was timed in an earlier run with the same settings.

sections.content: LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO. Our LIBERO evaluation uses ten tasks per suite and 50 official initial states per task.
